4.definition: A medieval Islamic financial instrument: a written order to pay a sum in another city, letting merchants move money across long distances without hauling coin — the direct ancestor of the modern bill of exchange.

One of the great Florentine banking houses (alongside the Bardi and Peruzzi) that bankrolled European kings in the early 1300s — and collapsed in the 1340s when Edward III of England defaulted on his war debts.

7.definition: From the Latin lectio ("reading"), the core teaching method of the medieval university: a master read a designated authoritative text aloud, sentence by sentence, pausing to gloss difficult words and untangle the argument while students copied it all down. Together with the disputation (a structured oral debate) it formed the backbone of scholastic instruction.
